$purpose: A finalized privacy-pass token is sealed to the server's X25519 token-encryption key so relay
operators cannot read spent tokens in transit. The client only ever seals; the server only
ever opens. That asymmetry is why this format went unchecked: no single repository held both
halves, and each side's tests proved it agreed with itself.
Three implementations existed until 2026-08-27 — iOS ServerKeyManager.sealBox, the core's
pp_seal_token_bytes, and the server's opener — under one doc comment in the core claiming it
'matches iOS ... and construct-server's ...'. iOS now calls the core. These vectors are the
check the comment was standing in for.
A seal the server cannot open is `decrypt_failed`: fatal under enforce, and under permissive
indistinguishable from ordinary anti-abuse degradation, which is why it could ship broken.
$construction: 1. eph = fresh X25519 keypair, per seal. shared = X25519(eph_priv, server_pub).
2. key = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = shared, salt = EMPTY, info = 'construct-token-seal-v1', len = 32).
The salt is absent, not zero-length-and-meaningful: RFC 5869 substitutes HashLen zero bytes,
and HMAC pads any key shorter than its 64-byte block with zeros, so an implementation that
passes an empty salt and one that passes 32 zero bytes derive the same key. Both spellings
are in the field (CryptoKit takes Data(), the hkdf crate takes None) and they agree.
3. nonce = 12 fresh random bytes. ct_and_tag = ChaCha20-Poly1305(key, nonce, token), IETF
Overhead is exactly 60 bytes; a sealed token is len(token) + 60.
$why_vectors_pin_the_opener: Sealing is randomised — a fresh ephemeral key and a fresh nonce per call — so no fixed byte
string can test a sealer, and two correct sealers never produce equal output. What a vector
can pin is an OPENER: given this server secret and these bytes, this plaintext must come out.
A client that only seals still uses these: it writes an opener in its own primitives, checks
it against these vectors, and then checks its own sealer against that opener. That is the
chain TokenSealDifferentialTests runs on iOS, and it is what caught nothing on 2026-08-27 —
the two sealers did agree, which is a result worth having recorded rather than assumed.

vectors.name: 32-byte token
vectors.note: the shape a real token has; sealed is 92 bytes = 32 + 12 + 32 + 16

vectors.name: 64-byte token
vectors.note: every plaintext byte distinct, so a reversed or misaligned ciphertext slice cannot open by luck
